ety.text: From Middle English multitude, multitud, multytude (“(great) amount or number of people or things; multitudinous”), borrowed from Old French multitude (“crowd of people; diversity, wide range”), or directly from its etymon Latin multitūdō (“great amount or number of people or things”), from multus (“many; much”) + -tūdō (suffix forming abstract nouns indicating a state or condition). The English word is analysable as multi- + -itude.

senses.d: A great amount or number, often of people; abundance, myriad, profusion.
ex: Do I contradict myself? / Very well then I contradict myself, / (I am large, I contain multitudes.)

senses.d: The mass of ordinary people; the masses, the populace.
ex: Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil
